Week One Grammar: Use of conjunctions Reading Comprehension Composition: Paragraphing (development of paragraph) Literature: Review of literary terms/devices LESSON 1: GRAMMAR TOPIC: USE OF CONJUNCTIONS (ALTHOUGH AND WHEREAS) TOPIC: CONJUNCTIONS 1. Definition of a Conjunction A conjunction is a word used to join words, phrases, or clauses together in a sentence. In simple terms, conjunctions are “joining words.” Examples: 1. I bought bread and butter. 2. She was tired but she continued working. 3. We stayed at home because it was raining. 2. Uses of Conjunctions Conjunctions help us to: 1. Add information Example: Mary and John came to school. 2. Show contrast (difference) Example: He is rich but unhappy. 3. Give reasons Example: She cried because she was hurt. 4. Show choice or alternatives Example: You can have tea or coffee. 5. Show time Example: I will call you when I arrive. 6. Show condition Example: I will go if you go with me. 7. Make sentences flow better They help avoid short, choppy sentences. Types of Conjunctions There are three main types of conjunctions:

Coordinating Conjunctions These conjunctions join words or clauses of equal importance. You can remember them using the acronym: FANBOYS a. For b. And c. Nor d. But e. Or f. Yet g. So Examples: a. I wanted to go, but it was late. b. She likes rice and beans. c. Hurry up, or you will miss the bus. B. Subordinating Conjunctions These join a main clause (independent clause) to a subordinate clause (dependent clause). They show relationships like time, reason, condition, result, etc. Common examples: because, although, if, when, while, since, unless, before, after Examples: a. I stayed indoors because it was raining. b. Although he is young, he is very wise. c. I will help you if you ask me. C. Correlative Conjunctions These are used in pairs to join equal parts of a sentence. Common pairs: a. either…or b. neither…nor c. both…and d. not only…but also Examples: a. Either you study hard or you fail. b. Both the teacher and the students were present. c. She is not only intelligent but also hardworking. 4. Important Notes a. A conjunction helps to avoid repetition. b. Do not overuse conjunctions in a sentence.

c. Ensure correct punctuation when joining clauses. 5. Examples in Sentences a. The boy is poor but honest. b. I didn’t come to school because I was sick. c. Although it was raining, they continued playing. d. You can stay here or go home. 6. Common Errors to Avoid Wrong: Because he was tired. (Incomplete sentence) Correct: He slept because he was tired. Wrong: She likes rice and but beans. Correct: She likes rice and beans. Exercise A. Fill in the blanks with suitable conjunctions: 1. I will go ___ you come with me. 2. She is poor ___ happy. 3. We stayed indoors ___ it was raining. 4. You can take tea ___ coffee. B. State the type of conjunction used: 1. I was late because of traffic. 2. He tried hard but failed. 3. Either you apologize or you leave. TOPIC: PARAGRAPHING Definition of a Paragraph A paragraph is a group of sentences that develop one main idea. It begins with a topic sentence and is supported by other sentences that explain or give more details. Example: My school is very beautiful. It has large classrooms and a clean environment. The teachers are friendly and hardworking. I enjoy learning there. Parts of a Paragraph A good paragraph is made up of three main parts: i. Topic Sentence

This is the first sentence of the paragraph. It introduces the main idea, in other words, a topic sentence is the main sentence in a paragraph that tells the reader what the paragraph is about. It usually comes at the beginning of the paragraph. Simple Explanation Think of a topic sentence as a headline for your paragraph. It introduces the main idea, while the other sentences give more details. Example Topic sentence: My school is a wonderful place to learn. Supporting sentences: a. The teachers are very friendly. b. The classrooms are neat and spacious. c. There are many learning materials available. Key Features of a Topic Sentence A good topic sentence: a. States the main idea clearly b. Is not too long or too short c. Is specific, not too general Another Example Playing football is good for students. (All other sentences in the paragraph will explain why or how football is good.) Example: Football is my favourite sport. Supporting Sentences These sentences explain, describe, or give details about the topic sentence. They may include examples, reasons, facts, explanations, etc. Example: a. I play it every weekend with my friends. b. It helps me stay fit and active. c. I also enjoy watching matches on television.

Concluding sentence: This is the last sentence. It summarises the paragraph or gives a final thought. Example That is why football is very important to me. LITERATURE TOPIC: LITERARY TERMS/DEVICES Objectives: At the end of the lesson, students should be able to: i. Define literary terms and figures of speech ii. Define all the literary terms and figures of speech under study. iii. Identify them in any work of art. CONTENT: LITERARY TERMS FLASHBACK: A flashback is an interruption in a narrative that depicts events that have already occurred, either before the present time or before the time at which the narration takes place. IRONY: is when a statement is used to express an opposite meaning than the one literally expressed by it. This occurs when the opposite of what is expected is realized. Examples Paul is the most intelligent boy in the class yet he comes last. Peter is very wealthy yet he borrows from beggars. There are three types of irony VERBAL IRONY: this means when someone says something but means the opposite (similar to sarcasm) SITUATIONAL IRONY: This is when something happens that’s the opposite of what was expected or intended to happen. DRAMATIC IRONY: When the audience is aware of the true intentions or outcomes, while the characters are not.

ALLEGORY: An allegory is a story that is used to represent a more general message about real-life (historical) issues and/ or events. It is typically an entire book, novel, play, etc. MOOD: Mood is a general feeling the writer wants the audience to have. The writer can achieve this through description, setting, dialogue, and word choice. ASSIGNMENT Define Character and Characterisation. FIGURES OF SPEECH The figures of speech are various devices that are used to give non-literal meanings. They are used to create rhetoric effect. There are a number of figures of speech in literature, but a few are used in the English language tests. Some of them include the following: 1) Simile 2) Metaphor 3) Personification 4) Hyperbole 5) Euphemism 6) Rhetorical question 7) Onomatopoeia Simile: this is a form of comparison between two things, which are generally not alike but in a particular aspect are alike. These things are compared using ‘as’ and ‘like’. Examples: Damilola is like a dove. (Meaning Damilola is gentle). Kayode is as fast as a hare. (Meaning Kayode is very fast). Metaphor: this is also a type of comparison but unlike the simile, it’s a direct comparison. While the simile says someone is like something else, the metaphor says the person is the exact thing. It is used without the use of either ‘like’ or ‘as’. Examples: Damilola is a dove. Kayode is a hare. Hyperbole: this is a deliberate exaggeration of fact or truth. It is otherwise called overstatement. Examples: I have warned you a million and one times. He could devour a mountain of rice if he is hungry. Euphemism: it is a subtle way to say something unpleasant in a pleasant manner. Examples: May I visit the comfort station? (Meaning “may I go to the toilet?”). The king has kicked the bucket. (Meaning “the king is dead”).

Rhetorical Question: this is a question that does not necessarily need an answer. It is used for curiosity and emphasis sake. Examples Are you out of your mind? Is God not faithful? Onomatopoeia: this is a figure of speech that has its meaning in sound. Examples The crowing of cocks. The booming of guns. Personification: this is the figure of speech that gives inanimate objects the animate qualities. Examples: The sky is crying. (Meaning “it is raining”). His pen is dancing on the paper. (Meaning “he is writing”). Assignment. 1. Give an example of the following figures of speech a. Personification b. Simile c. Oxymoron d. Metaphor e. Onomatopoeia WEEK 2 LESSON 1: GRAMMAR Week Two Grammar: Conjunctions Reading Comprehension Literature: Summary of recommended prose text Composition: Paragraphing (development of paragraph) Paragraphs Continued: How Paragraphs Are Built (Steps in Writing a Paragraph) 1. Choose a Topic Decide what you want to write about. Example topics

a. My Best Friend b. My School c. A Memorable Day 2. Think of Main Ideas Write down points related to your topic. 3. Write a Topic Sentence Introduce the main idea clearly. 4. Add Supporting Details Explain your idea using examples, descriptions, reasons 5. Arrange Ideas Logically Make sure your ideas flow in a clear order: From simple to complex From general to specific 6. Write a Concluding Sentence End the paragraph properly. 4. Qualities of a Good Paragraph A good paragraph should have: Unity All sentences must relate to one main idea. Wrong: Mixing different ideas Correct: Focus on one topic only B. Coherence Ideas should be well organised and flow smoothly. Use linking words like: and, but, because, however, also

C. Adequate Development The paragraph should have enough details to explain the idea clearly. D. Correct Grammar and Punctuation Use proper: a. Capital letters b. Full stops c. Correct spelling 5. Types of Paragraphs A. Narrative Paragraph Tells a story or event. Example: A story about your holiday. B. Descriptive Paragraph Describes a person, place, or thing. Example: Describing your classroom. C. Expository Paragraph Explains or gives information. Example: How to cook rice. D. Argumentative Paragraph Gives opinions and supports them. Example: Why students should wear uniforms. Example of a Complete Paragraph: My best friend is a very kind person. She always helps me with my schoolwork when I find it difficult. She is honest and never tells lies. We play together during break time and share our lunch. I am happy to have such a wonderful friend.

7. Common Errors to Avoid Writing too many ideas in one paragraph. Focus on one idea No topic sentence. Start with a clear main idea. Poor organization. Arrange ideas logically No conclusion. End with a proper closing sentence 8. Exercise Write a paragraph (8–10 sentences) on any of the following topics: a. My Favourite Teacher b. A Visit to the Market c. Why I Love My School Identify the parts of the paragraph below: Lagos is a busy city. Many people live and work there every day. The roads are always full of cars and buses. There are many markets and offices. It is one of the most active cities in Nigeria. Topic sentence: __________ Supporting sentences: __________ Concluding sentence: __________ Conclusion Paragraphing is an important writing skill. It helps you to organise your ideas clearly so that readers can easily understand your message. LITERATURE TOPIC: POPULAR THEMES IN MYTHS AND LEGEND OBJECTIVES: At the end of the lesson, students should be able to: Define theme Mention some of the popular themes in myths Discuss some of the popular themes in legends.

CONTENT: Myths and legends are important to us today for a number of reasons. They have value as literature, offering timeless and universal themes; they give us insight into other times and places; and they help us to see how much humankind had and has in common. The themes of myths and legends are the same as those that are present in all great literature, just a few of which are man versus man, man versus nature, man versus the gods, man on a quest, family conflict, and coming of age. Most myths and legends include at least one of these great themes and often several. These are in the earliest "stories," the ancestors of all literature that we read today. Even aside from the beauty and creativity of these stories, which alone make them worthy of study, they enrich our study of literature today to see its earliest roots. Every culture has its own mythology and legends and these reflect the geography of the culture, the values of the culture, and the history of the culture. Japanese creation myths, for example, reflect the fact that Japan is an island nation, and the sea and its creatures play an important part in these myths. Myths can also tell us what a culture considers ethical, significant, and central to its ideologies, giving us insight into another culture. A culture's myths, such as those of some Native Americans, tell us something about its history, the history of peoples that were hunters and gatherers, people whose governing forms did not sanction private ownership of land or disrespect the natural world. Each myth you read has something to tell you about another culture. But in spite of the differences we see in various myths and legends, it is good to know that deep down, people are the same. We want to know how we came to be, we want to understand the natural world around us, and we yearn for some deity we can praise and blame. Some popular themes in myths and legends include: 1. Heroism 2. Faith 3. Fate 4. Love 5. Sacrifice 6. Generosity GRAMMAR VERBS: USE OF HAVE, HAS AND HAD Objectives: At the end of the lesson, students should be able to:

i. Identify the figure of speech these words are. ii. Use them in sentence construction. iii. State their differences. CONTENT: The three belong to the family of the verbs ‘to-have’ under the primary auxiliary verbs. ‘Has’ is used when the subject of the sentence is singular, expressing a present tense while ‘Have’ is used when the subject of the sentence is plural and also expresses the present tense. ‘Had’ is the past form/tense of both has/have. It is used with both singular and plural subjects. • PRESENT TENSE: I/you/we/they = have he/she/it/Tobi /director= has • PAST TENSE (SIMPLE) I/you/we/they/he/she/it/Ada/chairman = had • FUTURE TENSE (SIMPLE) I/you/we/they/he/she/it/Ada/director = will have • PRESENT PERFECT ‘Have’ or ‘Has’ is used with a past participle to form the present perfect tense. • PAST PERFECT The past perfect is formed with ‘had’ and a past participle. PRESENT PERFECT CONTINUOUS Subject + have / has + been + Present Participle (verb + ing) • PAST PERFECT CONTINUOUS Subject + had + been + Present Participle (verb + ing) • FUTURE PERFECT CONTINUOUS Subject + will + have + been + Present Participle (verb + ing) Note: The Present Participle and Past Participle for the verb “be” (is, am, are) is been.

Here are some sentence examples to help portray the differences. Have I have a great job. I have an Oxford dictionary. I have blue eyes. I have a great boss. Has She has a horrible job. He has the biggest oxford dictionary. She has green eyes. He has a mean boss. Had I had a great job before the economic crisis. Now I am unemployed. He had an Oxford dictionary but someone stole it last week. I had blue eyes when I was born but they changed to brown when I was two years old. I had a great boss in my old company. ASSIGNMENT. Change the following sentences to present perfect and past perfect tenses. 1. The cat drinks milk. 2. He writes letters. 3. She bakes cake. 4. Assembly begins at 8 am. 5. She cooks for a living. TOPIC: LETTER WRITING (FORMAL) OBJECTIVES: At the end of the lesson, students should be able to: i. Define letter writing ii. Define formal letter. iii. Mention the features of a formal letter.

iv. Mention the category of people formal letter is written to. CONTENT: A formal letter is a letter one writes to offices to a. request for something b. apply for a job c. complain about faulty purchases d. give your opinion on a controversial issue. Such letters are usually written to business houses, ministries, institutions and newspaper houses. They are addressed to heads of such places, such as the chairman; the Registrar; the Principal; the Editor, etc. A formal letter is also known as an official letter or an impersonal letter. In this regard, you must be strictly official. Go straight to the point and be brief. Use official language – no short forms, no slang, no greetings. Alpha Choice Innovative Academy; Arepo, Ogun state. 25th May, 2024. The Editor, Vanguard Newspapers, P.M.B. 1007, Apapa, Lagos State. Sir, Examination Malpractice – Immediate Action Now! I wish to contribute to the on-going debate in your newspaper on how to stop examination malpractice in our society. It is very sad and disgraceful that up till now, we have not found a solution to that problem. I agree with Mr. David Oke, which article captioned “More Drastic Steps” appeared in your issue of 2nd August, that stricter measures be applied; not minding whose child is affected. The law against examination malpractice should not exempt anybody and must be applied, if we are serious. Drastic measures, if taken, will serve as deterrents and prevent a lot more from involving themselves in examination malpractice. Action now, if we want to curb examination malpractice! Yours faithfully, Mba Eunice

Essential Tips Writing Formal Letters 1. Use two addresses, the writer’s address and the recipient’s address. 2. Punctuate those addresses well. No date after the second address. 3. Open with “Sir”, “Madam”, or “Dear Sir”, “Dear Madam”. 4. Give a heading/title of your letter and underline. You can write all in capital letters and then you do not underline. 5. Go straight to the point. No exchange of pleasantries. 6. Be official. No short forms, no slang, no colloquial expressions. Be brief, no embellishments. 7. Close with “Yours faithfully” – capital “Y” small “f”, then comma. 8. Write your signature. 9. Write your full names – Your name and your surname followed by a full stop. ASSIGNMENT. Write a letter to the chairman of your local government council, expressing your dissatisfaction with the achievement of his regime so far, and pointing out two major problems of your people which require his urgent attention. TOPIC: EXPOSITORY ESSAY Objectives: At the end of the lesson, students should be able to: i. Define expository essay. ii. Mention the features of an expository essay. iii. Write a good expository essay. CONTENT: An expository essay is a genre of writing which tends to explain, illustrate, clarify, or explicate something in a way that it becomes clear for reader. Therefore, it becomes clear for readers. Useful hints on how to write a good expository essay 1. Discuss at length the topic you are asked to discuss. In most cases, you are expected to unfold the bad and good consequences of the topic. 2. There should be an introduction and conclusion. The introduction must briefly explain the main idea of the essay and it must be followed by the body of the essay. 3. You are expected to arrange your points or ideas in a logical sequence. 4. Your sentence should be variety of long and short sentence. 5. Make use of phrases or word linkers to link your paragraph with one another. 6. Clarity of expression is important. You must make sure that you state your facts, instances. 7. Your vocabulary should be carefully chosen for effectiveness, especially when you are writing on a topic that has a formal register. 8. Your language should be formal; you should avoid slangs, clothes, unidiomatic expressions and meaningless phrases. ASSIGNMENT Write an expository essay titled “Juvenile delinquencies; causes, effect and solution”. WEEK 5 LESSON 1: GRAMMAR TOPIC: VERBS Verbs are words that express an action or a state of being. CONTENT A descriptive essay describes so many things such as person, a place, a scene, an event or an object. A good descriptive essay brings what is described so close that the person to whom we describe will have a clear picture of what object or person. Description is writing what something or somebody is. Listeners or readers will understand you better when you are able to describe well, using appropriate words. In the same manner as other types of essays, your writing must have introduction, body and conclusion. 1) In the introductory paragraph, you mention the scene, object or person you want to describe, the general features and the outward appearance. If you are describing a place. 2] Make use of well-developed paragraphs 3] There must be logical sequence of arrangement of the features and qualities of what you are describing. 4] Your paragraphs must be effectively linked for unity and coherence. 5] Make use of appropriate words which will best convey your description to your readers. 6] There must be clarity of expression. 7] Probe yourself by generating questions that will help you develop the essay. These questions will lead you to write the required essay length.

Define synonyms and antonyms ii. Give word examples and their synonyms and antonyms. iii. Use each word in a sentence construction. iv. CONTENT SYNONYMS Generally, synonyms are looked at as words, whose meanings are the same. Although linguists are in agreement that no two words have exactly the same meaning in the English language. The correct way to define synonyms, therefore, should be --- words that have almost identical/similar meanings, although they may have subtle differences. Let us see these words--- wealthy and rich as examples. Both have almost identical meanings, yet they have a subtle difference; whereas the former refers to a position of affluence and apply mainly to human beings, the latter has its meaning extended to having any ingredient or quality in great abundance, productive, etc. It can therefore be applied to even inanimate things; hence, we may say ‘rich soil’, ‘rich tea’, ‘rich song’, etc. Examples. Abandon- desert, forsake, leave Abode- dwelling- place, home, habitation, residence Actual- existing, real Ally- friend, helper, partner. Anxiety- misgiving, uneasiness. Candid- frank, outspoken, sincere, straightforward.

Charity- benevolent, philanthropy Fussy- fastidious, particular, meticulous. Gay- blithe, cheerful, jolly, merry. Gloom- darkness, depression, melancholy. govern- control, rule Increase- amplify, augment, expand, magnify. see- behold, discern, perceive, scan trick- deception, pretense, hypocrisy suitable- appropriate, befitting Ugly- grotesque, horrid, unsightful. Souvenir- memento, relic, remembrance. Rash- careless, hasty, reckless Joke- banter, jest. Infinite- boundless, endless. Assignment. Write out the synonyms of the following words. 1) calamity 2) gloom 3) thrifty 4) foreboding 5) mitigate 6) Incarcerate 7) assemble 8) flimsy 9) revolt 10) destitute.

Antonyms Antonyms explain the idea of oppositeness. But, just as we mentioned while treating synonyms, there’s no perfect antonym. To be free from the difficulty of antonyms, students should first learn how the words are formed. Opposites (antonyms) are most commonly formed by adding PREFIXES to root words e.g. a + moral = amoral il + legal = illegal im + possible = impossible non + sense = nonsense un + usual = unusual in + active inactive ir + relavant irrelevant dis + honest dishonest Other prefixes to perform opposites are dis – (dishonorable), in - (incomplete), ir – (irresponsible The suffix – less is also used to form antonyms: e.g. mother + less = motherless Point + less = pointless Value +less = valueless Always check the meaning of words before you use them. Give the meaning and antonyms of each of the following words. (i) recalcitrant (ii) opaque (iii) benediction (iv) recommendation (v) accordance

WEEK 7 MID TERM BREAK WEEK 8 LESSON 1: GRAMMAR TOPIC: PREFIX AND SUFFIX Essential Questions: i. What is a Prefix? ii. What is a suffix? iii. How are they used? CONTENT: Words with a different grammatical form or meaning can be derived from a base word using prefixes and suffixes. By understanding how these prefixes and suffixes work, it is often easier to deal with unknown vocabulary. You can sometimes see what part of

speech a word is (verb, noun, adjective etc.), or additional information that a prefix may give. 1. Changes in grammatical form. The noun 'power' can be used as an adjective by adding the suffix ‘ful’ (powerful). The adverbial form is made by adding the suffix -ly to the adjective (powerfully). The verb 'to improve' becomes a noun by adding the suffix -ment (improvement). The same root word can also become a verb (improvise). The noun 'nation' changes into an adjective with the suffix -al (national), and by adding another suffix -ize the word changes from an adjective to a verb (nationalize). The adjective 'special' can change to a verb (specialize) or a noun (specialty). 2. Changes in meaning. Affix can also change the meaning of a word. There are two types of affix; Prefix is added before a root word while suffix is added after a root word. The meaning of 'possible' is reversed with the addition of the prefix im- (impossible). To 'overeat' means to eat too much and if food is undercooked, it is not cooked enough. Some suffixes commonly denote an occupation. The verb 'to teach' is transformed into the occupation with the suffix -er (teacher). Both grammatical changes and changes in meaning can be applied to the same base word. Eg. The noun 'interest' can be made an adjective and given opposite meaning by adding a prefix and a suffix -un -ing (uninteresting). 3. Changes in pronunciation. When prefixes and suffixes are added to root words, the word stress sometimes changes, examples Noun & verb: 'photograph'. Adjective: 'photographic'. Opposite: 'unphotographic'. Person: 'photographer'. In English the word stress is often on the third syllable from the end. Prefixes Prefixes are first syllables like “non-” and “re-” that have their own meaning. They combine with words to create new meanings. Pre + View = Preview (first look). Super + Star = Superstar (top player). Prefixes add meaning to thousands of words. Learn a few prefixes, and you open up the meaning of thousands of words. The four most frequent prefixes are 97% of prefixed words! Most Common Prefixes 1. a = without: amoral, apolitical, atypical

2. ante = before: antecedent, antedate 3. anti = against, opposing: anti-war, anti-bacterial 4. arch = more extreme: arch-capitalist, arch-rebel 5. auto = self: auto-dial, auto-rotate 6. bi = two, twice: bilingual, bisect, bi-monthly 7. circum = round: circumnavigate, circumvent 8. co = with: co-author, co-edit 9. col, com, con = with: collaborate, combine, connect 10. contra, counter = against, opposing: contraception, counter-claim 11. de = opposite action: declassify, destroy 12. dia = across: diagonal, diameter 13. dis = not, opposite of: disagree, disprove, distrust, disbelief 14. dys = abnormal: dyslexia, dysfunctional 15. e = electronic: e-literate, e-book 16. eco = relating to the environment: eco-tourism, eco-disaster 17. en(m) = cause to: encode, embrace 18. equi = equal: equidistant, equilateral 19. ex = previously: ex-president, ex-student 20. extra = very: extra-bright, extra-strong 21. extra = outside: extra-curricular, extra-sensory 22. fore = before: forecast 23. hyper = having too much: hyperactive, hypersensitive 24. il, im, in, ir = not: illogical, impossible, indistinct, irrational 25. in(m) = in, movement to: input, inset, intake, implant, import 26. inter = between, connected: interrelated, interact 27. intra = within: intra-generational, intramuscular 28. kilo = thousand: kilogram, kilometer, kilowatt 29. macro = large in size or scope: macro-economics, macro-scale 30. mal = badly: malfunction, malpractice 31. micro = small in size or scope: micro-economics, micro-scale 32. mid = middle: midway 33. mis = wrongly : mistake, mistranslate, misunderstanding 34. mono = one : mono-centric, monoculture 35. multi = many : multicultural, multi-level 36. neo = based on something older but in new form : neo-classical 37. non = not : non-believer, non-competitive, nonsense 38. out = more, to a greater extent : outnumber, outlive 39. over = over/above/too much : overlook, overcook, overhead 40. post = after : post-examination, post-modern 41. pre = before : pre-industrial, preview, pre-war

Educate LESSON 2 TOPIC: FUNDAMENTAL ELEMENTS OF PROSE OBJECTIVES: By the end of this lesson, students should be able to: Say what the elements of prose are Identify some fundamental elements of prose in any given text Apply the knowledge in writing their own stories/prose CONTENT 1. Plot: the sequence of events in a literary work [Gustav Freytag, of Freytag's Pyramid fame, enumerated a typical sequence of plot events: introduction, rising action, climax, falling action and catastrophe (now often termed denouement). Some variations of plot include flashbacks and "flash forwards." Story is the raw material of which plot is constructed. According to E.M. Forster, "the king died and the queen died" is a story, whereas "the king died and then the queen died of grief" is a plot because it emphasizes causality. Hmmmm?

2. Theme: not simply the subject of a literary work, but rather a statement that the text seems to be making about that subject. So the subject of a novel might be suffering; the theme, depending on the view of the individual author, might be that suffering is in God's plan and should therefore simply be accepted. English teachers make use of many synonyms for theme: main idea, gist, central concept, message, moral, lesson or perspective (to name few). 3. Motif: a unifying element in an artistic work, especially any recurrent image, symbol, theme, character type, subject or narrative detail. (Not to be confused with motive.) Specific colors such as green and white serve as motifs in Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby. 4. Setting: that combination of place, historical time, and social milieu that provides the general background for the characters and plot of a literary work. 5. Narrator: a speaker through whom an author presents a narrative, often but not always a character in the work point of view/perspective: the vantage point from which a narrative is told first person ("I") third person (omniscient or limited) reliable unreliable 6. Style: the way in which a literary work is written, the devices the author uses to express his or her thoughts and convey the work's subject matter syntax structure 7. Tone (voice): the attitude of the author toward the reader or the subject matter 8. Mood/Atmosphere: the general feeling created in the reader by a work at a given point. OBJECTIVES: At the end of the lesson, students should be able to; 1) Define tag questions 2) Mention types of tag questions 3) Identify the correct tag to a statement. A tag question is a grammatical structure in which a declarative or an imperative statement is turned into a question by the addition of an interrogative fragment. A tag question is also a question added to a declarative sentence usually at the end, to engage the listener, verify that something has been understood, or confirm that an action has occurred. The two basic rules about tag questions are: if the statement is negative, the tag must be positive. If the statement is positive the tag must be negative. For example In the sentence “You’re John, aren’t you? Is turned into a question by the tag aren’t you. In English, there are four types of questions: general or yes/no questions, special questions using wh- words, choice questions, and distinctive or tag/ tail questions. Question tags are used to keep a conversation going. You can agree or refuse to a sentence with a question tag Affirmative sentence: He is from Germany, isn’t he? Negative sentence: He isn’t from Germany, is he? He never goes out with his dog, does he? We have a car, don’t we? Lets take the next bus, shall we? More examples Students must work hard, musn’t they? You will not say no to my request, wiil you? I love my parents, don’t i? You will go, wont you? You speak French don’t you? LESSON 2 TOPIC: REVIEW OF LANGUAGE SKILLS. Skills relate to different aspects of using language, such as listening, reading, speaking, and writing. Skills are our ability to do these things. They are usually divided into two types; receptive and productive What are receptive and productive skills? Receptive skills are those used in understanding reading or listening. Productive skills involve producing language; speaking or writing. The four basic language skills are: Listening: When people are learning a new language they first hear it spoken Speaking: Eventually, they try to repeat what they have heard. Reading: Later, they see the spoken language depicted symbolically in print. Writing: Finally, they reproduce these symbols on paper. Listening, speaking, reading and writing are the four language skills we need to develop for complete communication. Listening and reading are receptive: input, i.e. The exposure you have to authentic language in use. Assignment. 1) Why is listening important in communication? 2) How can one develop the four skills? TOPIC: COMPONENTS OF LETTER WRITING AND ESSAY WRITING. OBJECTIVES: At the end of the lesson, students should be able to; 1. Mention the components of composition. 2. Write short note on each component. All composition should have three important parts. These are the introduction, the body and the conclusion. These three parts must be present in all the composition you write. Use paragraphs to make these parts stand out in your work. INTRODUCTION This is the section at the beginning of your writing. It summarises or sets the scene for what you are about to write. BODY.

This is where you have the main part of your writing, that is, the points and ideas you want to pass across to the reader. CONCLUSION. This is the final part of your writing. It should be the final paragraph of your composition. You can conclude by summarising the important points you raised in the body of your composition. Your conclusion should be brief and interesting. OBJECTIVES: At the end of the lesson, students should be able to: 1) Define formal and informal letters 2) Write the format of these two letters. 3) Attempt any given question on these letters. INFORMAL LETTER The informal letter is a personal letter. It is a letter that is written to a friend, brother, sister, uncle, parents or any close acquaintance, discussing a personal, private or an intimate affair. There is familiarity and intimacy and the language is relaxed, sometimes chatty. Features/Format of an informal letter 1. The address of the writer, usually written at the top right-corner of the letter. 2. The date. 3. Salutation. 4. The body of the letter 5. Conclusion. 6. Subscript or closing. Assignment. Write a letter to your uncle telling him to assist your parents in paying your school fees. Give him three reasons why you want him to help you. FORMAL LETTER.

A formal letter, also known as a business letter, is a letter written in formal language with a specific structure and layout. Formal letters are generally used by businesses to communicate with other businesses and individuals. FEATURES OF A FORMAL LETTER Your address as the sender in the top right-hand corner; The receiver’s address on the left-hand side; The correct opening (Dear Sir/Madam, Dear Mr Smith, Dear Editor); Title A suitable and precisely worded opening sentence. Avoid opening with ‘I am writing to you…’ A number of well-developed paragraphs; A firm summing up of the purpose of the letter; Avoidance of shortened forms (e.g. I’m, don’t, won’t, etc.); The use of appropriate vocabulary; Conclusion A suitable and appropriate signing off (e.g. ‘Yours faithfully’ – very formal with Dear Sir’, ‘Yours sincerely’ – less formal with ‘Dear Mr. Pit'). ASSIGNMENT Write a letter to your Local Government Authority commenting on three health hazards in your area. Make suggestions as to how the situation can be improved. Preposition

A preposition is a word that shows the relationship between a noun or pronoun and another word in a sentence. In simple terms, a preposition helps us understand: Where something is When something happens How something happens Example: The book is on the table. She came after the lesson. Prepositions usually come before a noun or pronoun. Examples of Common Prepositions Some common prepositions include: in, on, at, under, above, between, beside, with, from, to, into, during, after, before Functions (Uses) of Prepositions Prepositions are used to show different kinds of relationships in sentences: Position / Place (Where?) Shows location or position. Examples: The bag is under the chair. The teacher is in the classroom. The boy stood beside his friend. Time (When?)

Shows time of an action. Examples: The meeting starts at 10 a.m. We shall travel in December. She arrived after the test. Direction / Movement (Where to?) Shows movement from one place to another. Examples: She is going to school. The cat jumped onto the table. He walked into the room. Manner / Means (How?) Shows how something is done. Examples: He wrote the letter with a pen. She travelled by bus. Types of Prepositions Prepositions of Place Examples: in, on, under, between, behind, near The keys are in the drawer. Prepositions of Time

Examples: at, on, in, during, before, after The exam is on Monday. Prepositions of Direction Examples: to, into, onto, from, across The children ran across the field. Prepositions of Manner / Instrument Examples: with, by, in She cut the paper with scissors. Compound Prepositions These are made up of more than one word. Examples: because of in front of out of according to Example: He succeeded because of hard work. Prepositional Phrase A prepositional phrase consists of; A preposition + its object (noun/pronoun) Examples:

on the table in the classroom under the bed Rules for Using Prepositions A preposition is always followed by a noun or pronoun. Correct: She is fond of music Wrong: She is fond of Avoid unnecessary repetition: Wrong: Where are you at? Correct: Where are you? Some prepositions depend on usage (fixed expressions): examples Afraid of Interested in Good at Common Errors to Avoid He discussed about the issue. He discussed the issue. She entered into the room. She entered the room. Importance of Prepositions Prepositions are important because they:

Make sentences clear and meaningful Help in proper communication Improve writing and speaking skills Class Drill A. Fill in the blanks with correct prepositions: 1. The cat is ___ the table. 2. We arrived ___ night. 3. She walked ___ the room. 4. The boy is sitting ___ his friend. B. Identify the prepositions in the following sentences 1. The book is on the desk. 2. She came after the meeting. 3. He ran into the house. Make sentences using the following: In, under, between, during Summary A preposition shows the relationship between words. It usually comes before a noun or pronoun. It expresses ideas such as place, time, direction, and manner. .
